sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Shallow foundations generally bear at depth less than about 2 times the foundation width. Understanding the theoretical assumptions behind design procedures matters more than the exact definition. Common types include isolated footings, strip footings, cantilever stemwall footings, combination footings, and mat foundations, illustrated in Figures 2-1 through 2-5.
sections.body: (p. 5) The definition of a 'shallow foundation' varies from author to author but generally is thought of as a foundation that bears at a depth less than about two times the foundation width. The definition is less important than understanding the theoretical assumptions behind the various design procedures. It is important to recognize the theoretical limitations of a design procedure that may vary as a function of depth, such as a bearing capacity equation. Common types of shallow foundations are shown in Figures 2-1 through 2-5.
key_points: Shallow foundation generally defined as bearing depth less than about 2 times the foundation width
Understanding theoretical assumptions behind design procedures is more important than the strict definition
Bearing capacity equations have theoretical limitations that vary as a function of depth
Common types illustrated in Figures 2-1 through 2-5
sections.applicability: General classification and definition of shallow foundations for all design applications.

sections.title: Isolated Spread Footings
sections.summary: Isolated spread footings distribute a single column's concentrated load to prevent shear failure of the bearing material and limit settlement. For bridge columns they are typically greater than 3 m by 3 m (10 ft by 10 ft), larger for eccentric loads. Size depends on the column loads and the bearing materials' strength and compressibility; structural design covers moment at the column face and in the short direction, shear and punching around the column.
sections.body: (p. 5) Isolated spread footings (Figure 2-1) are designed to distribute the concentrated loads delivered by a single column to prevent shear failure of the bearing material beneath the footing and to minimize settlement by reducing the applied bearing stress. The forces, strength and plan dimensions of the column may govern the minimum size of an isolated spread footing. For bridge columns, isolated spread footings are typically greater than 3 m by 3 m (10 ft by 10 ft). These dimensions will increase when eccentric loads are distributed to the footing. The size of the footing is a function of the loads distributed by the supported column and the strength and compressibility characteristics of the bearing materials beneath the footing. Structural design of the footing includes consideration for moment resistance at the face of the column and in the short direction of the footing, as well as shear and punching around the column.
key_points: Designed to distribute concentrated column loads and prevent shear failure of bearing material
Typical minimum size for bridge columns is 3 m x 3 m (10 ft x 10 ft)
Footing size increases with eccentric loads
Sizing depends on column loads and bearing material strength/compressibility
Structural design considers moment resistance at column face, shear, and punching shear
sections.applicability: Single column support where loads can be distributed to adequate bearing material through an individual footing.

sections.title: Continuous Strip Spread Footings
sections.summary: Most common foundation type for buildings; supports a single row of columns or a bearing wall with a minimum length-to-width ratio of 5:1. Plane strain conditions assumed parallel to the long axis. Structural design governed by beam shear and bending moments. Can tie columns together in one direction and reduce pressure on bearing materials.
sections.body: (p. 6) The most commonly used type of foundation for buildings is the continuous strip spread footing (Figure 2-2). Continuous or strip footings generally have a minimum length to width ratio of at least 5 (i.e., length > 5 x width). They support a single row of columns or a bearing wall to reduce the pressure on the bearing materials. These footings may tie columns together in one direction. Sizing and structural design considerations are similar to isolated spread footings with the exception that plane strain conditions are assumed to exist in the direction parallel to the long axis of the footing. The structural design of these footings is generally governed by beam shear and bending moments.
key_points: Most common foundation type for buildings
Minimum length-to-width ratio of at least 5 (length > 5 x width)
Supports a single row of columns or a bearing wall
Plane strain conditions assumed parallel to the long axis
Structural design governed by beam shear and bending moments
Can tie columns together in one direction
sections.applicability: Support of bearing walls or a single row of columns where continuous load distribution is needed.

sections.title: Spread Footings with Cantilever Stemwalls
sections.summary: Combines vertical load distribution with retaining wall function. Foundation resists eccentric loads; lateral earth pressures are resisted by cantilever action of the stemwall and overturning resistance of the footing. Three sub-applications: bridge abutments, semi-gravity retaining structures, and building foundations with basement or buried walls.
sections.body: (p. 6) When a spread footing with a bearing wall is used to resist lateral loads applied by backfill, the foundation and the wall must perform both vertical load distribution and retaining wall functions. The foundation is designed to resist the resulting eccentric load, and the lateral earth pressures are resisted by cantilever action of the stemwall and overturning resistance provided by the footing. This section covers three sub-applications: bridge abutments, retaining structures, and building foundations.
key_points: Combines vertical load distribution with retaining wall function
Foundation must resist eccentric loads from lateral earth pressures
Lateral pressures resisted by cantilever action of stemwall and overturning resistance of footing
Three main sub-applications: bridge abutments, retaining structures, and building foundations
sections.applicability: Situations where shallow foundations must resist both vertical loads and lateral earth pressures from backfill.

sections.title: Bridge Abutments
sections.summary: Bridge abutments must retain backfill, support the superstructure and distribute loads to bearing materials, provide an approach fill transition, and accommodate thermal movements. Spread footings with cantilever stemwalls are well suited for these multiple simultaneous functions.
sections.body: (pp. 6-7) Bridge abutments are required to perform numerous functions: retain the earthen backfill behind the abutment, support the superstructure and distribute the loads to the bearing materials below the spread footing, provide a transition to the approach fill, and depending on structure type, accommodate shrinkage and temperature movements within the superstructure. Spread footings with cantilever stemwalls are well suited to performing these multiple functions. The general arrangement of a bridge abutment with spread footing and cantilever stemwall is shown in Figure 2-3.
key_points: Abutments must retain backfill, support superstructure, provide approach fill transition, and accommodate thermal movements
Spread footings with cantilever stemwalls are well suited for these multiple functions
Must distribute superstructure loads to bearing materials below the footing
figures: Figure 2-3: Spread Footing with Cantilever Stemwall at Bridge Abutment (p. 7)
sections.applicability: Bridge abutment design where the foundation must serve both structural support and earth retention functions.

sections.title: Retaining Structures
sections.summary: Semi-gravity cantilever retaining walls (inverted T-walls) use shallow spread footings as their base. Stability derives from the dead weight of backfill on the heel and from structural cantilever action of the stem. The footing acts as both a foundation element and a stabilizing element resisting overturning.
sections.body: (p. 7) The bases of semi-gravity concrete cantilever retaining walls (inverted 'T' walls) are essentially shallow spread footings. The wall derives its ability to resist loads from a combination of the dead weight of the backfill on the heel of the wall footing and the structural cantilever of the stem (Figure 2-4).
key_points: Semi-gravity cantilever retaining walls (inverted T-walls) use shallow spread footings as their base
The wall resists loads by the dead weight of backfill on the heel and the structural cantilever of the stem
sections.applicability: Semi-gravity concrete cantilever retaining wall design where the base footing provides foundation support and overturning resistance.

sections.title: Building Foundations
sections.summary: Building stemwalls resist lateral earth pressures when buried or partially buried as basement walls. Unlike bridge abutments and cantilever walls, tops and ends of building stemwalls are frequently restrained by beams, floors, and transverse interior walls, providing additional structural resistance beyond cantilever action.
sections.body: (p. 7) When a building stemwall is buried, partially buried or acts as a basement wall, the stemwall resists the lateral earth pressures of the backfill. Unlike bridge abutments and semi-gravity cantilever walls, the tops or the ends of the stemwalls are frequently restrained by other structural members (e.g., beams, floors, transverse interior walls, etc.) to provide additional structural resistance.
key_points: Building stemwalls resist lateral earth pressures when buried or partially buried
Tops and ends of stemwalls are often restrained by beams, floors, or interior walls
Additional structural restraint differentiates building foundations from bridge abutments and cantilever walls
sections.applicability: Building foundations with basement walls or buried stemwalls that must resist lateral earth pressures with additional structural restraint.

sections.title: Combination Footings
sections.summary: Combination footings support two or more columns on a rectangular or trapezoidal footing; used where column spacing is non-uniform or isolated footings become so closely spaced that one footing is simpler to build. The spill-through abutment is a bridge example, used on early Interstate alignments on competent native soil and at stream crossings to keep foundations below scour. Frame action lets them resist large overturning moments along the column row.
sections.body: (pp. 8-9) Combination, or combined, footings are similar to isolated spread footings except that they support two or more columns and are rectangular or trapezoidal in shape (Figure 2-5). They are primarily used when the column spacing is non-uniform (Bowles, 1996) or when isolated spread footings become so closely spaced that a combination footing is simpler to form and construct. In the case of bridge abutments, an example of a combination footing is the so-called 'spill-through' type abutment (Figure 2-6). This configuration was used during some of the initial construction of the Interstate freeways on new alignments where spread footings could be founded on competent native soils. Spill-through abutments are also used at stream crossings to make sure foundations are below the scour level of the stream. Due to the frame action that develops with combination footings, they can be used to resist large overturning or rotational moments in the longitudinal direction of the column row. Design depends on available space, load distribution among columns, variations of soil properties, and economics.
key_points: Support two or more columns on a single rectangular or trapezoidal footing
Used when column spacing is non-uniform (Bowles, 1996) or isolated footings become so closely spaced that a combined footing is simpler to form and build
Spill-through abutments are a bridge application of combination footings (Figure 2-6)
Frame action allows resistance to large overturning or rotational moments
Spill-through abutments used at stream crossings to place foundations below scour level
Design choice depends on available space, load distribution, soil variability, and economics
figures: Figure 2-6: Spill-Through Abutment on Combination Strip Footing (p. 9)
sections.applicability: Multiple-column support where individual footings would overlap or where non-uniform column spacing or large overturning moments are present.

sections.title: Mat Foundations
sections.summary: Single heavily reinforced concrete slab underlying the entire structure; economical when spread footings would cover more than about 50% of plan area (Peck et al. 1974). Principal advantage is bridging over soft spots and reducing differential movement. Limited bridge application; more common for maintenance facilities, storage bins, and box culverts in transportation. Large mat design discussed in Section 8.6.
sections.body: (p. 10) A mat foundation consists of a single heavily reinforced concrete slab which underlies the entire structure or a major portion of the structure. Mat foundations are often economical when spread footings would cover more than about 50 percent of the footprint of the plan area of a structure (Peck et al. 1974). A mat (Figure 2-7) typically supports a number of columns and/or walls in either direction or a uniformly distributed load (i.e., tank). The principal advantage of a mat foundation is its ability to bridge over soft spots and reduce differential movement. Structures founded on relatively weak soils or lightweight structures may be economically supported on mat foundations. Mat foundations distribute loads over a large area, reducing contact pressures. They are designed with sufficient reinforcement and thickness to be rigid enough to distribute column and wall loads, minimizing differential settlements and tolerating larger uniform settlements. Often the mat also serves as the base floor level of building structures. Mat foundations have limited applicability for bridge support, except where large bridge piers, such as bascules or other movable bridge supports, have the opportunity to bear at relatively shallow depth without deep foundation support. Discussion of large mat foundation design is included in Section 8.6. A more common application of mat foundations to transportation structures might include lightly loaded rest or maintenance facilities such as small masonry block structures or sand storage bins or sheds, or box culverts constructed as a continuous structure.
key_points: Single heavily reinforced concrete slab underlying the entire structure or major portion
Economical when spread footings would cover more than about 50% of the plan area (Peck et al. 1974)
Principal advantage is ability to bridge over soft spots and reduce differential movement
Suitable for relatively weak soils or lightweight structures
Limited applicability for bridge support; applicable for bascule piers and movable bridge supports
Common transportation applications include maintenance facilities, storage bins, and box culverts
Large mat foundation design discussed in Section 8.6
sections.applicability: Structures where spread footings would cover more than 50% of the plan area, or where differential settlement must be minimized over weak or variable ground conditions.

sections.title: Shallow Foundations in Performance Applications
sections.summary: High quality case histories for shallow foundations in transportation are scarce due to lack of post-construction settlement monitoring. DiMillio (1982) documents several relevant cases. Three new case histories illustrate cost savings from spread footings in compacted engineered fills and competent natural ground, highlighting the importance of investigation and monitoring.
sections.body: (p. 11) High quality case histories regarding shallow foundations in transportation applications are difficult to obtain, largely because settlement data following construction are often not recorded. Several relevant case histories are documented in 'Performance of Highway Bridge Abutments on Spread Footings' (DiMillio, 1982). Three new case histories are included to highlight design and construction practices that take advantage of the cost savings available by constructing spread footings in compacted engineered fills and in competent natural ground.
key_points: Case histories for shallow foundations in transportation are scarce due to lack of post-construction settlement monitoring
DiMillio (1982) documents several relevant case histories
Three new case histories demonstrate cost savings from spread footings in compacted fills and competent ground
Case histories highlight importance of thorough site investigation and construction monitoring
sections.applicability: Evaluation of shallow foundation performance in transportation applications through case history review.

sections.title: Case History No. 1: I-5 Kalama Interchange, Washington
sections.summary: 71-m four-span prestressed concrete bridge on 30 m of compressible alluvial sediments (Cc = 0.19–0.24). Two-stage preloading with up to 14.6 m of fill; post-deck settlement 21–49 mm; maximum angular distortion under 0.002. Eliminated 124 timber piles, saving approximately $25,000 (about 20% of total structure cost).
sections.body: (pp. 11-16) During Interstate construction in the 1960s and 1970s the Washington State Highway Commission (later WSDOT) built many bridges on spread footings, many on structural fills (DiMillio, 1982). This case shows the savings from thorough site investigation, laboratory testing, sound geotechnical engineering and follow-through in construction with the observational method (Peck, 1969): settlement measured against time during a delay period after the approach embankment was built was used to judge the feasibility of footings at the abutments and to predict their long-term settlement. The bridge is a 71-m (233-ft) long, 8.5-m (28-ft) wide, four-span prestressed concrete structure carrying east-west traffic across Interstate 5 in Kalama, southwestern Washington, on Piers 1 to 5 (WSDOT calls abutments piers, so Piers 1 and 5 are the abutments; Figure 2-8), built in 1968 and 1969. About 30 m (100 ft) of alluvium (interbedded loose to medium dense sand, soft to medium stiff silt, occasional peat) overlies bedrock (Figure 2-9). Three consolidation tests (Table 2-1): moisture 46-50 percent, moist unit weight 16.5-17.1 kN/m3, Cc = 0.19-0.24. Given the depth of compressible soil and the cost of deep foundations, the Commission used conventional spread footings with preloading before the footings were built; one year of preload was allowed in the schedule. At least 3 m (10 ft) of compacted granular fill was kept below the interior pier footings and up to 14 m (45 ft) placed at the abutments. Footings were sized for 3 tsf, WSDOT's presumptive value for fills of Gravel Borrow (specification in Appendix A); the actual design pressures were 280 kPa (2.9 tsf) at Piers 1 to 4 and 244 kPa (2.55 tsf) at Pier 5. The preload went on in two stages so the soil gained strength and to reduce instability: Stage 1, as much as 7.6 m (25 ft), finished in mid-October 1967; Stage 2 about 6 months later; total about 13 m (43 ft) at Pier 1, 14.6 m (48 ft) at Pier 5 and about 7.6 m (25 ft) at the interior piers. By late June 1968, 0.34 m (1.1 ft) and 0.9 m (3.0 ft) had settled under the preload at Piers 1 and 5. Piers 3 to 5 were built in August 1968; Piers 1 and 2 waited until November 1968 because the approach fills were still settling too fast. The deck was finished in December 1968 and monitored monthly for 4 months: by April 1969, 37 to 49 mm (0.12 to 0.16 ft) at the abutments and 21 to 34 mm (0.07 to 0.11 ft) at the interior piers (Table 2-2, Figure 2-10), fairly uniform, with maximum angular distortion between adjacent piers below 0.002. The project was completed in June 1969 and has performed well for more than 30 years (Figure 2-11). Costs: at $20 per square foot (inflation adjusted, WSDOT 1975 data) the contract was about $130,000; a project memorandum put the saving from spread footings instead of 124 timber piles 15 to 18 m (50 to 60 ft) long at about $25,000, about 20 percent of the structure cost.
key_points: 71-m (233-ft), four-span prestressed concrete bridge over I-5 at Kalama, built 1968-1969

At least 3 m of compacted granular fill below interior pier footings; up to 14 m at the abutments
Sized for 3 tsf (WSDOT presumptive for Gravel Borrow); design 280 kPa (2.9 tsf) Piers 1-4, 244 kPa (2.55 tsf) Pier 5
Post-deck settlement to April 1969: 37-49 mm at abutments, 21-34 mm at interior piers; angular distortion below 0.002
Spread footings instead of 124 timber piles saved about $25,000, about 20% of the $130,000 structure
Observational method (Peck, 1969): settlement monitored during a delay period to judge feasibility

sections.title: Case History No. 2: I-580 Mt. Rose Highway Interchange, Nevada
sections.summary: 107.6-m two-span concrete bridge on dense glacial outwash and alluvial fan deposits (SPT N 25–75, avg 50). Design bearing pressure 190 kPa (2 tsf); estimated settlement 32–57 mm; groundwater >30 m deep. Abutments on compacted aggregate base structural fill (95% MDD). Cost savings of $105,000 (4% of $2.8 million) by eliminating piles.
sections.body: (pp. 16-19) The northbound I-580 overpass over Mt. Rose Highway, Washoe County, Nevada, built in 1994: 107.6 m (353 ft) long, 25.8 m (84.5 ft) wide, two concrete spans on two end abutments and an intermediate pier, all on spread footings (Figure 2-12). The site lies in Donner Lake Glacial Outwash and Mt. Rose Alluvial Fan Deposits (SHB AGRA, 1993; 10 borings). North abutment: dense, fine- to medium-grained silty sand to sand with gravels and cobbles, SPT N-values generally 25 to 75, average 50. Center pier: from about 0.6 to 7.6 m (2 to 25 ft) a medium dense to very dense silty sand to sand with gravels and occasional cobbles, underlain by 1.5 to 3.0 m (5 to 10 ft) of low to medium plasticity, hard clayey sand to clayey gravel grading into very dense sandy gravel. South abutment: dense to very dense silty sand to sand with gravels. Groundwater was not encountered and is believed deeper than 30 m (100 ft). Estimated settlements at a design bearing pressure of 190 kPa (2 tsf) were 32 mm at the abutments and 44 to 57 mm at the center pier, considered tolerable, so spread footings were chosen. On the sloping terrain the abutment footings bear on both cut and structural fill (up to about 2.5 m, 8 ft); the center pier is on natural ground (Figure 2-13). The fill was compacted aggregate base (Nevada DOT Type 1 Class B): crushed rock, 100 percent passing 37.5 mm (1-1/2 in.) and 1 to 12 percent passing 75 um (No. 200) (Appendix A), in lifts of at most 200 mm (8 in.) compacted to 95 percent of maximum density by Nev. T101 (Harvard Miniature Compaction Device). Figure 2-14 shows the south abutment footing. Settlement was not monitored; Nevada DOT reports no problems since construction. Costs: the project (about 7.2 km, 4.5 mi of Interstate) cost about $52.9 million and was paid by unit prices, so bridge costs cannot be compared directly; with piles at $1,000 each to drive plus $65 per 0.3 m (1 ft) of pipe pile, about 20 piles 7.5 m (25 ft) long at each abutment would have cost about $105,000; at about $1,000 per square meter the structure cost about $2.8 million, so footings in compacted structural fill saved at least 4 percent.

Abutments on cut and up to 2.5 m of Type 1 Class B aggregate base, 200 mm lifts, 95% of maximum density (Nev. T101)
Deleting about 20 piles per abutment saved about $105,000, at least 4% of the $2.8 million structure
Not monitored; Nevada DOT reports no problems since construction

sections.title: Case History No. 3: Cadillac Bypass Structure S01, Michigan
sections.summary: Structure S01 of the Cadillac Bypass (US-131, Michigan): a 77.8-m (255.4-ft) three-span concrete bridge on loose sand up to 6 m thick over medium dense to very dense sand. Abutment footings bear on about 7.6 m of Structure Embankment placed on the existing ground after topsoil removal; under the piers the loose soil was removed and replaced, over 4.6 m in all. Fill: granular, 0-15% passing No. 200, 230-380 mm lifts, 100% of the maximum unit weight. Saving about $180,000 (about 8% of $2.3 million), about 18 piles per pier.
sections.body: (pp. 20-21) The Cadillac Bypass project involves extending the limited-access US-131 around Cadillac to Manton, Michigan. The project includes 24 structures, 10 of which are or will be supported on spread footings. Structure S01, the northbound US-131 relocation overpass over S-43 Road, is 77.8 m (255.4 ft) long and 14.7 m (48.3 ft) wide, a three-span concrete structure with two abutments and two piers (Figure 2-15). Subsurface conditions consist of a loose sand layer up to about 6 m (20 ft) thick, underlain by medium dense to very dense sand with trace fine gravel. Three of the four borings were dry at completion; the fourth had water 2.4 m (8 ft) below the ground surface. Abutment and pier footings were placed on structural fill (Michigan DOT designation: Structure Embankment), placed on existing ground after topsoil removal. Thickness of Structure Embankment was about 7.6 m (25 ft) under abutment footings and over 4.6 m (15 ft) under pier footings. Loose soils were removed from under pier locations and backfilled with Structure Embankment. The Structure Embankment consisted of granular material: 100% passing 150 mm (6 in) sieve, 95-100% passing 75 mm (3 in), 0-15% passing 75 um (No. 200). Placed in lifts of 230-380 mm (9-15 in) and compacted to 100% of Maximum Unit Weight (equivalent to Modified Proctor Method). Settlement has not been monitored. The whole project is estimated at $117 million and is scheduled for completion in 2004. Estimated cost savings of about $180,000 (about 8% of the $2.3 million structure cost), based on deletion of approximately 18 piles per pier at $2,500 per in-place pile.

sections.title: Pre-Cast Foundation Elements, Mudsills and Temporary Footings
sections.summary: Temporary falsework foundations do not require frost protection but must still be designed against shear failure and excessive settlement using the same analytical procedures as permanent structures (Chapters 5–6). ASTM 1194/AASHTO 235 plate load tests are commonly required to verify capacity. Caution is needed when a stiff crust overlies softer soils, since the plate's depth of influence is less than that of the actual foundation.
sections.body: (p. 22) Many bridges require temporary support, or falsework, in order to complete the permanent structure. Falsework is in turn supported on temporary foundations. Because they are temporary, these foundations do not need the same design considerations as permanent structures. For instance, frost protection is usually not required, so temporary footings can bear at shallow depth or directly on the ground surface. However, the temporary footing still must be designed to limit stress applied to the supporting soil to prevent shear failure (see Section 5.2) and to limit settlement to a tolerable amount (Section 5.3). The analytical procedures for checking performance are the same as for permanent structures (Chapters 5 and 6). Many transportation agencies require a field plate load test (ASTM Test Method 1194 and AASHTO test method 235 are identical) to confirm the load-carrying capacity and settlement of falsework foundations. Plate load test data should be used with caution when a stiff, near surface crust overlies softer, saturated soils, since the depth of influence (see Section 3.1.5) will be less for the plate than the actual falsework foundations. In this case, site-specific settlement analyses should be required.
key_points: Temporary foundations for falsework do not require frost protection
Must still be designed against shear failure and excessive settlement
Same analytical procedures as permanent structures (Chapters 5 and 6)
ASTM 1194 / AASHTO 235 plate load test commonly required to verify capacity
Plate load test data should be used with caution when stiff crust overlies softer soils
Depth of influence for plate test is less than for actual foundations; site-specific analysis may be needed
sections.applicability: Temporary falsework foundations and mudsills for bridge construction where simplified design is acceptable but bearing capacity and settlement still require verification.
